title: Spontaneous and tension pneumothorax
subtitle: Symptoms and risk, not size alone, decide the intervention

sources.title: British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease
British Thoracic Society Clinical Statement on pleural procedures

sources.org: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma
sources.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual

red_flags.text: Tension: respiratory distress, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, absent breath sounds, and in the ventilated patient rising airway pressures. Tracheal deviation is late.
High-risk characteristics: haemodynamic compromise, significant hypoxia, bilateral pneumothorax, underlying lung disease, age 50 or over with a significant smoking history, or haemopneumothorax.
Pneumothorax in a patient about to be ventilated or to fly. Positive pressure and altitude both expand it.
Recurrent pneumothorax, or a pneumothorax around the menses: consider catamenial disease and refer.

do_now.text: Suspected tension pneumothorax: decompress immediately on clinical grounds, without waiting for a radiograph, then place a chest drain.
In adults, needle decompression is placed in the fourth or fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line; finger thoracostomy in the ventilated trauma patient.
High-flow oxygen for hypoxia, titrated to target saturations, especially with chronic lung disease.

assess.text: Decide primary (no known lung disease) or secondary (underlying lung disease, or age 50 or over with significant smoking history).
Assess symptoms, breathlessness and the patient's priorities. In the BTS 2023 pathway, symptoms and high-risk features drive treatment more than radiological size.
Look for subcutaneous emphysema, bilateral signs and haemodynamic compromise.

investigate.text: Erect posteroanterior chest radiograph. Measure and record the size for trend, but do not let size alone decide treatment.
CT chest when the radiograph is unclear, a bulla is suspected, or for complex or recurrent disease and surgical planning.
Thoracic ultrasound can detect a pneumothorax at the bedside in experienced hands.

resuscitate.text: Primary pneumothorax with minimal symptoms and no high-risk features: conservative management with clear safety-net advice and follow-up is an option.
Symptomatic primary pneumothorax needing intervention: needle aspiration, an ambulatory device, or a small-bore chest drain, chosen with the patient.
Secondary pneumothorax: admit. Most need a small-bore chest drain; observe all patients in hospital.

definitive.text: Insert drains in the safe triangle, with a small-bore Seldinger drain first-line. Never clamp a bubbling drain.
Persistent air leak or failure to re-expand: early respiratory and thoracic surgical review. Suction or an endobronchial valve may be options in selected patients.
Offer definitive surgery (VATS with pleurectomy or pleural abrasion) for a recurrence, a first contralateral episode, bilateral pneumothorax, persistent air leak, and in high-risk occupations.
Advise no flying until the pneumothorax has resolved and been confirmed, and avoid diving permanently unless definitive surgery has been performed.

escalate.text: Senior help for tension, bilateral pneumothorax, or pneumothorax in a ventilated patient.
Respiratory team for every secondary pneumothorax; thoracic surgeons for persistent air leak and recurrence.
Smoking cessation for every patient: smoking increases recurrence substantially.

notes: Tension is a clinical diagnosis. The radiograph of a tension pneumothorax should never exist.
In a young patient with a large primary pneumothorax and few symptoms, doing less is often the right answer.
A secondary pneumothorax with a small rim on the film can still kill a patient with poor lung reserve.
